raw_case_text:
An 11-year-old girl of Arab origin was diagnosed with ataxia telangiectasia (AT) at 1 year of age. Her parents are first cousins; both are healthy. She has four siblings, one of which was diagnosed with AT, as well as some other family members.
In her early childhood, the patient suffered from ataxia and repeated lung and ear infections. She also developed sclerosing cholangitis and hypothyroidism. In later years, she used a wheelchair for mobility. Eventually, she was diagnosed with diffuse large B cell lymphoma.
Lymphocyte count and function-normal, decreased immunoglobulins-IgG (516 mg/L).
Monthly IVIG, inhalations (budesonide, fluticasone propionate), and levothyroxine.
Multiple cafe-au-lait spots and telangiectasias.
At 11 years, the patient developed a spreading skin rash on her nose. The lesions spread to the nostrils and her left cheek.
Initially, she was treated with amoxicillin and clavulanic acid and a topical antibiotic (chloramphenicol), however, with no response.
Upon examination, on the tip of the nose, there was an erythematous plaque with a central erosion and a circinate-elevated border with overlying scattered pustules. The nose bridge and nostrils had small erythematous erosions (Figure 4).
An atypical infection was suspected. The result of a PCR test for Leishmania was negative. A mycological test showed hyphae, but a species could not be identified due to a small sample.
She was then treated with oral fluconazole 5 mg/kg for 4 weeks and a topical combination antibiotic and antifungal treatment (ciclopirox, gentamicin) with a good response but with remaining lesions in the nostrils. At this point, erythematous plaques with a gold crust were seen around the nostrils and impetigo was suspected. Repeated cultures grew Staphylococcus aureus and Candida.
Fluconazole, cephalexin, and nasal bacitracin were given, with improvement seen in the patient's condition, but frequent impetigo recurrences followed. She was therefore started with prophylactic treatment of cephalexin for 1 month with resolution and no recurrences.
AT patients rarely acquire opportunistic infections, although they may be more susceptible to viral infections (HSV, VZV, Human papillomavirus (HPV) warts, molluscum). Their T cell function may be relatively intact, thus explaining the uncommon occurrence of opportunistic infections. A case report described an AT patient with an invasive candida infection due to a functionally impaired T cell function. Our case was a diagnostic challenge. Due to residence in an endemic region, leishmaniasis was initially high on the differential, but eventually, clinical suspicion and fungal cultures were of help.

subjective.chief_complaint: An 11-year-old girl of Arab origin presented with a spreading skin rash on her nose extending to the nostrils and left cheek.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: At 11 years of age, the patient developed a spreading skin rash on her nose that progressed to involve the nostrils and her left cheek. She was initially treated with oral amoxicillin-clavulanic acid and topical chloramphenicol without clinical response.
subjective.past_medical_history: Diagnosed with ataxia telangiectasia (AT) at 1 year of age; history of early childhood ataxia, recurrent lung and ear infections, sclerosing cholangitis, hypothyroidism, wheelchair dependence for mobility, and diffuse large B-cell lymphoma. Born to healthy first-cousin parents; one of four siblings and several other relatives also diagnosed with AT. Resides in a leishmaniasis-endemic region.
subjective.review_of_systems: Home medications include monthly intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG), inhaled budesonide and fluticasone propionate, and oral levothyroxine.

objective.physical_examination: Multiple cafe-au-lait spots and telangiectasias. On the tip of the nose, there was an erythematous plaque with a central erosion and a circinate elevated border with overlying scattered pustules; small erythematous erosions were present on the nasal bridge and nostrils (later evolving to erythematous plaques with golden crusts around the nostrils).
objective.advanced_workup: Immunological workup showed normal lymphocyte count and function with decreased serum IgG (516 mg/L).

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Cutaneous leishmaniasis was initially suspected due to residence in an endemic area, but Leishmania PCR was negative. Mycological microscopy revealed fungal hyphae, and subsequent repeated cultures of residual crusted nostril lesions grew Candida and Staphylococcus aureus, confirming cutaneous candidiasis with recurrent secondary impetigo. Treatment with oral fluconazole (5 mg/kg for 4 weeks) and topical ciclopirox/gentamicin led to initial improvement, followed by fluconazole, cephalexin, and nasal bacitracin, and finally a 1-month prophylactic course of oral cephalexin that achieved complete resolution without further recurrence.
